hops.title: Brain organoids that grew primitive eye structures
hops.text: Some human brain organoids can organize the beginnings of an eye. In 2021, a team in Düsseldorf found that around day 30, some of their human brain organoids began assembling a pair of optic vesicles, the early structures of the eye, plainly visible by day 60. Inside were lens-like and corneal-like cells, retinal pigment epithelium, retinal progenitors and electrically active networks of neurons. Light of different strengths set off electrical activity in the tissue, and after bright light bleached it, its sensitivity came back. The tissue clearly responds to light; whether those signals are passed on and used by the rest of the organoid is still an open question.

sources.citation: Gabriel et al., Cell Stem Cell 28(10):1740–1757.e8 (2021), PMID 34407456.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A small translucent organoid in a glass Petri dish on a bench, with two tiny dark spots side by side on one side, under a gentle beam of light.
image.caption: In culture, some human brain organoids organize their own paired, light-sensitive eye structures.

hops.title: Skin cells from an old donor make young neurons
hops.text: A reasonable guess: skin cells from an 89-year-old should give you old neurons in a dish. That depends on how you make the neurons. In 2015, a Salk Institute team took skin fibroblasts from 19 donors aged 0 to 89 and reprogrammed 16 of the lines into iPS cells with the four Yamanaka factors. The iPS cells, and neurons made from them, lost most of the donors' age-linked gene signatures, and reprogramming even restored the separation of proteins between nucleus and cytoplasm in the iPS cells. When the team skipped the stem-cell stage and converted skin cells directly into neurons, those neurons still showed age-linked signatures.

sources.citation: Mertens et al., Cell Stem Cell 17(6):705–718 (2015), PMCID PMC5929130.
Mertens et al., Cell Stem Cell 17(6):705–718 (2015), PMID 26456686.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A wooden desk clock with blurred, backward-moving hands next to a glass dish of small young cell clusters on a sunlit table.
image.caption: Neurons made through a pluripotent stem-cell stage showed far fewer age-linked gene-expression differences than directly converted neurons.

hops.title: Cancer-linked TP53 mutations found in stem cell lines
hops.text: In 2017, a Harvard and Broad Institute team sequenced 140 human embryonic stem cell lines, 26 of them prepared for possible clinical use, and found an unwelcome passenger. Five unrelated lines carried six mutations in TP53, a tumor-suppressor gene often mutated in human cancers. Mining published RNA-seq data from 117 pluripotent lines turned up another nine. In three lines followed over time, the mutant copies of TP53 generally became more common as the cells were grown and split, which suggests the mutation gave its carriers an advantage in culture. The authors warned that changes like these can go unnoticed in most uses of a line.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A row of clear culture flasks on an incubator shelf, with bright amber cells crowding out pale blue cells inside one flask beside a magnifying glass.
image.caption: A mutation picked up in culture can spread through a stem cell line without anyone noticing.
